text.p: Global commodity markets took a breather last Friday, settling in narrow price bands after some volatile roller-coaster rides earlier in the week.
Precious and industrial metals stabilised after hitting fresh lows earlier in the week.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index rose 0.13 points to 245.97.

Copper prices rose on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Friday in response to another sizeable drawdown in stocks, but finished the afternoon kerb session off the day's highs. Benchmark three month copper futures ended the kerb at $1,911 a tonne, up $15 from Thursday's close but $7 below the day's high. Aluminium prices gained ground in sympathy with copper, shrugging off a rise in stocks of 8,550 tonnes. Prices finished the afternoon kerb $5 higher at $1,357. The market traded in a narrow $4 range all day.
Nickel prices gained $70 to $7,170, boosted by a 306-tonne fall in stocks and news early in the day of an ongoing production stoppage at the WMC Rocky Reward mine in Australia.
Zinc nudged higher to $1,023 from $1,018.50 after stocks rose 325 tonnes. Lead rose $7 to $771 after stocks fell 250 tonnes.
Tin gained $75 to $6,095 after a stock decline of 95 tonne.
Alloy was last quoted at $1,210/15 from $1,208/10. Stocks fell 980 tonnes.

CBOT wheat futures closed mixed with nearby December coming alive in late dealings on bull spreading and commercial buying amid renewed talk about a tight supply of high quality soft red winter wheat in the United States, traders said. "We still need to attract good quality soft wheat to the eastern belt and that's why the spread is acting the way it is," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International. The December/March spread narrowed Friday to roughly 12-1/2 cents per bushel premium Dec, a 3-1/4 cent change from Thursday's close. Wheat closed one cent higher to five cents lower, with December up one at $4.21.

New York precious metals futures ended mixed Friday, with the month-long downtrend stalling for now, but the longer term outlook remaining bearish, analysts said. "The situation is deteriorating as the much delayed turn in economic activity in Europe and Japan has left the metals sector in surplus," Goldman Sachs commodities research director, Steve Strongin said. "At current demand levels inventories are building, providing a growing cushion against new demand when it finally arrives," he said. In bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted around $380.25 compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $380.70, and the New York close Thursday around $380.10.
Traders pushed NYMEX oil prices lower Friday in what some called a "breather" to recent sharp gains, and just like on the way up, crude oil and gasoline followed heat back down, traders said.
Heating oil for November delivery ended Friday 0.26 cent lower at 74.43 cents a gallon.
The trading session was characterized by profit taking tempered by views the bull run was not over.
Crude oil for November delivery meanwhile shed eight cents, settling at $24.73 a barrel, with no news in the market to give crude much influence in the trading rings, traders said.
Gasoline, with little or no influence on the market's tone, lagged the downward move, as November unleaded lost just 0.05 cent and settled at 63.63 cents a gallon.
